project.name: Idea to Customer
project.goal:
Find a software product worth building, build it, put it in front of its market, and take money from strangers before 31 December 2026. Paying customers are the only result that counts. Signups, waitlists, traffic, stars and compliments are leading indicators, and this company is not graded on leading indicators.

PHASE ONE IS A BAKE-OFF, NOT A BRAINSTORM. Produce five candidate ideas and research all five to the same depth before ranking any of them: what it is in two sentences; who specifically has the problem, named tightly enough that you could go find ten of them this week; what those people do about it today and what that costs them in money, time or risk; the market size with the arithmetic shown and every input sourced to something outside this company; what already exists, what it charges, and what its own paying users complain about in public; how it would reach buyers; what it costs to run per customer; and the cheapest test that would prove the whole thing wrong. Then choose one and write down why the other four lost. A killed idea with a reason is an asset. An unexamined one is a liability.

A BIAS, NOT A RULE: prefer something a consumer or prosumer buys on a card at a self-serve price, cheap to run and cheap to support, over something needing a sales cycle, a procurement process or a compliance review. If the strongest idea is the enterprise one, take it and argue for it — the ranking is on evidence, not on the chairman's taste.

THEN BUILD THE SMALLEST VERSION SOMEBODY WOULD PAY FOR, ship it where its buyers already are, and sell it. Distribution is this company's job. The chairman will not post about it, will not email his contacts, and will not introduce you to anyone. If the market hears about this product, it is because an agent here made that happen. Do not plan around his audience; for this purpose he does not have one.

EVERYTHING A STRANGER SEES HAS TO LOOK LIKE SOMEBODY CARED. This company is staffed by people who love interfaces and cannot leave an ugly one alone, and that is a hiring standard, not a preference: the landing page, the sign-up, the empty state, the pricing table, the receipt email and the error message are all the product, and a consumer decides whether to trust a thing they have never heard of in the first few seconds of looking at it. Functional-but-ugly is not a milestone on the way to good — it is the version that gets no second visit and teaches you nothing about whether the idea works, because you never find out whether they refused the product or refused the presentation. So: a design system before the second screen, one visual voice across the product and the marketing, both themes and both widths checked on the rendered page rather than argued about in a spec, and contrast, focus rings, touch targets and reflow treated as visual defects rather than as somebody else's accessibility checklist. The designer owns the bar. Everyone is held to it — an engineer shipping a screen nobody designed, or a marketer publishing a page that looks like a different company, is the same defect as a broken build. And it is a constraint on ambition, not a licence to gold-plate: pick a scope small enough that what you ship can be genuinely well made by the date.

ASK HIM FOR EXACTLY WHAT YOU CANNOT GET YOURSELF, and no more. A domain, a payment processor, a mailbox, hosting, a card for the recurring bills: file a need, say what it is for, what it costs, and what stops without it. If you can sign yourself up for a service and pay for it inside the spend envelope, do that instead of asking, and record the account you created. He is the enabler and the auditor of this company, never a member of it.

MONEY AND TIME ARE BOTH SHORT ON PURPOSE. The model budget is small while you are still deciding what to build, because a company that spends its year on research never ships; it will be raised at a review once there is something in the market that feeding would help. Read cheaply, write briefly, and put the tokens into the two things that are actually hard: finding out what is true outside this company, and getting a working product in front of somebody who might pay for it.

THE FINISH LINE is revenue booked through the payment processor's signed webhook — the platform's own record, not a claim in a status report. If 31 December arrives and nobody has paid, the deliverable is an honest post-mortem: which ideas died and on what evidence, what was actually built and shipped, what was tried in the market and what it returned, and what would have to be different for this to work. That is a real result and it will be read as one. What will not be accepted is a year of documents about a product nobody outside this company ever saw.
